In rustls 0.23.44 and 0.23.45, application data that a client buffers before the handshake completes is sent to the server even when the server rejects Encrypted Client Hello (ECH).

When the server rejects ECH, the client completes the handshake with the outer ClientHello and authenticates the server against the ECH config's `public_name`. At the end of the handshake, `start_traffic()` encrypts and queues any plaintext buffered by `ClientConnection::writer()`. It does this *before* checking for `EchStatus::Rejected` and queueing the `ech_required` alert.

The application then receives `Error::PeerIncompatible(ServerRejectedEncryptedClientHello)`, as expected. However, the client is still expected to call `write_tls()` to send the fatal alert, and that call also sends the encrypted application data. The server decrypts the data and only then receives the alert.

The ordering bug is older than 0.23.44. Before 0.23.44, the client checked the server certificate against the inner server name rather than `public_name`, so a correctly configured server failed certificate verification first and no data was sent. 0.23.44 fixed that check, which makes the ordinary rejection path reachable.

# Impact

Plaintext meant for the inner server, the one named in the encrypted ClientHello, goes to the client-facing server identified by `public_name`. That server is properly authenticated, so this is not an attack by an unauthenticated party. However this violates [RFC 9849](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9849), which says the following:

- Section 6.1.6: if the handshake and authentication succeed after ECH rejection, the client "MUST ... abort the connection with an "ech_required" alert **before sending any application data to the server.**"
- Section 6.1.7: the certificate is checked only against `public_name`, and the connection "MUST NOT" be reported as successful to the application. rustls does report failure correctly. The problem is only that data is sent before the alert.

This affects only clients that meet all of these conditions:

- They use `EchMode::Enable`. GREASE ECH is not affected.
- They write application data before the handshake completes.
- They connect to a server that rejects their ECH config, for example because the config is stale. This is the same case where the server returns retry configs.

The usual client response to rejection is to retry with the server's retry configs. In that case, the data has already gone to the outer server.

## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `better-auth` from 1.5.0-beta.12 through versions before 1.7.7 with the OAuth Proxy plugin. You are affected only if **all** of these are also true:

- On a participating environment, the OAuth Proxy plugin has no dedicated `secret`, or its `secret` equals that environment's global Better Auth secret.
- Sign-in state is stored in a cookie (`account.storeStateStrategy: "cookie"`). With a database or secondary storage, this is only the case if you chose it explicitly.
- Implicit account linking is on (the default).

You are not affected by this path if every participating environment uses a proxy `secret` distinct from its global Better Auth secret, if sign-in state is stored in the database, or if you use a version before 1.5.0-beta.12.

## Summary

The OAuth Proxy plugin trusts any user profile it can decrypt. In the affected setup, Better Auth encrypts sign-in state, including data the caller chose, with the same secret and hands it to anyone who starts a social sign-in. An attacker can use this to get a fake profile for another user's email address that the proxy accepts as real.

## Impact

An attacker without an account who knows a user's verified email address can sign in as that user, with that user's permissions. They can read private data, change the account, and link a provider account of their choice to it. They need no provider sign-in and no action from the victim. No availability impact is established, and a reported open redirect was not confirmed.

## Patches

The fix is merged for the planned `better-auth` 1.7.7 release. That package is not available yet.

Upgrade all nodes handling the same cookie-backed OAuth or SAML state flow and all OAuth Proxy participants together, including the production coordinator and preview or development deployments. Keep installed Better Auth packages released alongside `better-auth` on the same release version. Restart pending sign-in and account-linking flows; pre-upgrade state cookies and proxy payloads are rejected. Public options and API signatures are unchanged.

## Workarounds

Until you upgrade to the fixed release, apply one of these:

- Set one strong OAuth Proxy `secret` across every environment that takes part in the proxy flow, and keep it different from each environment's global Better Auth secret.
- Set `account.storeStateStrategy: "database"`. This is already the default when a database or secondary storage is configured. If Magic Link is also enabled, switching can expose a separate cross-purpose verification-record path in affected releases. Ensure the two flows resolve to distinct stored identifiers; with built-in options, use Magic Link `storeToken: "hashed"` with global `verification.storeIdentifier` unset or `"plain"`, or disable Magic Link or both built-in social and Generic OAuth sign-in.
- Remove the OAuth Proxy plugin if you do not need it.

Setting `account.accountLinking.disableImplicitLinking: true` stops this path from taking over an existing account. It does not fix the underlying flaw: the callback can still accept attacker-made data as a provider identity. Apply one of the steps above as well.

## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `better-auth` from `1.3.8-beta.3` up to, but not including, `1.7.0-rc.3`, and you enable the `deviceAuthorization()` plugin. This range includes all 1.6 releases.

You are affected only if all of these are also true:

- An attacker can start a device request: `validateClient` is not configured, or the attacker can use a valid public client.
- Before allowing approval, your approval page does not show, from server-checked data, which client is asking and the exact permissions it requests.
- Users may approve a code or complete verification link they did not start and cannot compare with a device they have.
- Your application accepts the session token that the device flow returns, for example through the bearer plugin.

You are not affected if you do not enable the opt-in `deviceAuthorization()` plugin.

## Summary

The device authorization plugin lets a user sign in on one device by approving a short code on another. In affected versions, the approval information given to the user leaves out which client asked for access and which permissions it wants. The official approval examples therefore show only a generic request and a code, so users cannot tell their own device from an attacker's request.

## Impact

An attacker who convinces a signed-in user to approve the attacker's code receives a live Better Auth session token for that user. The attacker can then read or change any data the user's account can access. The attack needs the opt-in device flow, a request the attacker creates, and a user who actively approves it; it is not a sign-in bypass without user action.

## Patches

The fix first shipped in `1.7.0-rc.3`. Upgrade to `better-auth@1.7.0` or later. No 1.6 release contains the fix.

After upgrading, `GET /device` returns the requesting `client_id` and `scope` to the signed-in account that owns the request. If you built your own approval page, update it to show that client and those permissions, and keep approval disabled until they load.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, do the following:

- Disable `deviceAuthorization()`, or block untrusted access to `/device/code`.
- Configure a strict `validateClient` allowlist. Do not rely on the allowlist alone: it limits who can start the flow, but it does not give users the missing approval information.
- Build your own approval endpoint. It should read the pending request from trusted server-side storage and map the checked client identifier to a trusted display name. Show the exact requested permissions and the user code. Keep approval disabled until this information loads.
- Tell users to reject device requests they did not expect. They should approve only when the same code is visible right now on a device they have.

## Technical details

A device starts the flow by calling `/device/code`. The plugin stores the client identifier and any requested scope with the pending request. Before approval, `GET /device` returns only the user code and its status. This is true even for a signed-in session of the user account that owns the request. An approval page built from that response cannot show which client asked for access or which permissions it wants. After approval, the original device code can be redeemed at `/device/token` for a Better Auth session token.

RFC 8628 describes this remote phishing scenario. It recommends that the server tell users they are authorizing a device and ask them to confirm that the device is in their possession. It also recommends showing device information that helps users detect impersonation. Client allowlisting reduces who can start the flow, but it does not give users the missing approval information. A valid public client can therefore still be affected when its identifier and requested permissions are not shown.

## Summary
`WekaClassifier` in NLTK passes a caller-controlled model file path to the weka Java VM without any `nltk.pathsec` validation. `WekaClassifier.train` puts the caller's `model_filename` verbatim into the weka argv `["-d", model_filename, ...]` (weka *writes* the trained model there), and `WekaClassifier._classify_many` puts `self._model` into `["-l", self._model, ...]` (weka *reads* it). Under `nltk.pathsec.ENFORCE=True` (the default on current HEAD), NLTK's stated invariant — established by advisory CVE-2026-81726 / GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp — is that caller-controlled model-artifact paths must be bounded to the allowed NLTK data roots before any native tool opens them. `WekaClassifier` is the one `java()`-based tool wrapper that skips this entirely, giving an untrusted workflow arbitrary-location file **write** (`-d`) and an arbitrary file **read/parse oracle** (`-l`), defeating pathsec containment.

This is a standalone, unfixed variant of the same class as CVE-2026-81726, on a code path the CVE-2026-81726 fix never touched. That advisory enumerates 6 functions (`TransitionParser.train`, `TransitionParser.parse`, `AveragedPerceptron.save`, `AveragedPerceptron.load`, `PerceptronTagger.save_to_json`, `save_maxent_params`) — `WekaClassifier` is not among them, and weka.py contains no `validate_tool_path`/`validate_model_resource` at all.

## Root Cause
`WekaClassifier.train(cls, model_filename, ...)` builds `cmd = [javaclass, "-d", model_filename, "-t", train_filename]` (nltk/classify/weka.py:256) and `WekaClassifier._classify_many` builds `[..., "-l", self._model, "-T", <staged>, ...]` (weka.py:131-133); `self._model` is stored unvalidated in `__init__` (weka.py:108-110). Only the internally-generated `train.arff`/`test.arff` are staged via `make_staging_dir`; the model path is passed as-is. `nltk.internals.java()` (internals.py:388-431) validates the classpath (`_verify_jar_sandbox`), the JVM launcher options (`_validate_java_options`, the CVE-2026-12841 fix), the main-class token `cmd[0]`, and rejects `@argfile` tokens in any position — but it explicitly permits program arguments starting with `-` and never inspects the interior of a program-arg path value. So `-d <path>` / `-l <path>` flow unchecked to `subprocess.Popen(final_cmd, shell=False)` and the weka JVM performs an unbounded native open/write on the caller-chosen path.

Sibling wrappers prove the intended pattern: `CRFTagger.train`/`set_model_file` call `validate_tool_path` (crf.py:134,300); `MaltParser.generate_malt_command` validates `-i`/`-o` via `validate_tool_path` (malt.py:340,344), its model via `validate_model_resource` (malt.py:326) and `working_dir` via `validate_path` (malt.py:206). weka.py already uses pathsec elsewhere (`validate_path` for WEKAHOME, `pathsec_open` for ARFF writes) but never for the model path.

## Impact
Under `pathsec.ENFORCE=True` (default on HEAD), an untrusted workflow that chooses the weka model save/load path obtains:
- Arbitrary-location file **write** via `-d` — overwrite or create a file at an attacker-chosen absolute or `..`-traversal path outside the allowed NLTK data roots (content constrained to weka's serialized-model format; the target choice is the integrity impact). This corrupts/clobbers arbitrary chosen files.
- Arbitrary file **read/parse oracle** via `-l` — weka loads an out-of-root path as a model, yielding an existence/parse differential (file content is not echoed back → confidentiality impact is limited).

This defeats the pathsec containment advisory CVE-2026-81726 promises, at the same privilege level / threat model that advisory was accepted under.

## Proof of Concept
```python
import nltk.pathsec as ps; ps.ENFORCE = True
from nltk.classify.weka import WekaClassifier
# write-side: model written OUTSIDE any allowed NLTK data root (refused for CRFTagger, allowed here)
WekaClassifier.train("/tmp/outside_sandbox/evil.model",
                     [({"a": 1}, "pos"), ({"a": 0}, "neg")])
# read-side: -l opens an arbitrary path
clf = WekaClassifier(fmt, "/home/victim/secret.model")
clf.classify_many([{"a": 1}])
```
The argv construction — the vulnerable step — is confirmed without weka installed (see Bypass Evidence); a configured weka.jar is needed only to observe the JVM's actual file I/O.

## Attack Chain
1. **Entry.** Action: an app running with `pathsec.ENFORCE=True` lets an untrusted workflow choose the weka model path and calls `WekaClassifier.train("../../../home/victim/x", featuresets)` (write) or `WekaClassifier(fmt, "/home/victim/secret.model").classify_many(...)` (read). Guard: none — plain classmethod/constructor parameter (weka.py:230,108-110). Bypass proof: grep shows weka.py uses no `validate_tool_path`/`validate_model_resource`/`validate_tool_dir` (NONE).
2. **Command build.** Action: the path is placed into `cmd = [javaclass, "-d", model_filename, "-t", train_filename]` (weka.py:256) / `["-l", self._model, ...]`. Guard: only the internally-generated `train.arff` is staged via `make_staging_dir`; the model path is passed as-is. Bypass proof: runtime capture yielded `['weka.classifiers.bayes.NaiveBayes', '-d', '/tmp/outside_sandbox_weka.model', '-t', '<staged>/train.arff']` — the raw out-of-root path is `cmd[2]`.
3. **java() sink.** Action: `java(cmd, classpath=_weka_classpath, ...)` → `subprocess.Popen(final_cmd)` (internals.py:431). Guard: `java()` validates classpath, JVM `options`, `cmd[0]`, and rejects `@argfile` tokens. Bypass proof: none of these inspect the `-d`/`-l` program-arg value; internals.py explicitly documents that program args after the main class may start with `-`, and the path is neither `cmd[0]` nor an `@`-token, so every `java()` gate passes. Negative control: the same path through `validate_tool_path(..., for_write=True, must_exist=False)` raises `PermissionError`.
4. **Impact.** Action: the weka JVM opens the path outside the allowed roots → arbitrary-location write (`-d`) / parse-existence oracle (`-l`). Guard: pathsec is never consulted (no `validate_tool_path`, no `pathsec_open`). Bypass proof: the directly-analogous sibling `CRFTagger.train` calls `validate_tool_path(model_file, must_exist=False)` (crf.py:300); weka does not, and commit `ee6d6138` hardened weka's other sinks (scratch files, WEKAHOME jar) while leaving the model path unvalidated.

## Bypass Evidence
- Negative control (guard is real): `validate_tool_path("/tmp/outside_sandbox_weka.model", for_write=True, must_exist=False)` → `PermissionError`; `validate_tool_path("../../../home/victim/.ssh/authorized_keys", ...)` → `PermissionError`.
- Sink reached unvalidated (guard absent): captured write-side argv `['weka.classifiers.bayes.NaiveBayes', '-d', '/tmp/outside_sandbox_weka.model', '-t', '<staged>/train.arff']` and read-side `[..., '-l', '/home/victim/secret.model', '-T', '<staged>/test.arff', '-p', '0']`.
- Version: `git show v3.10.3:nltk/classify/weka.py` contains both the `-d` model-path build (line 235) and the `-l` read, and NO `validate_tool_path`.

## Affected Versions
`<= 3.10.3` (present on the latest release tag v3.10.3 and on HEAD `c06cd264`). No published fix has ever targeted the weka `-d`/`-l` model path; commits after v3.10.3 (`ee6d6138`, `92aeada6`, `a9752559`) touched weka.py for other sinks but did not add model-path validation.

## Suggested Fix
Before building the `-d`/`-l`/`-T` command, validate the model path with pathsec, mirroring `CRFTagger`/`MaltParser`:
```python
validate_tool_path(model_filename, context="WekaClassifier.train", for_write=True, must_exist=False)
validate_tool_path(self._model, context="WekaClassifier._classify_many")
```


---
Reported by **zx (Jace)** — GitHub: @manus-use

## Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12 predates the fix).

PR: #3863 "Bound the WekaClassifier model path to the pathsec data roots", merged 2026-09-06, merge commit bc2878725 on develop. Fix commit: 6a1760629.

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_j456_xh4h_cpf2.py, added by PR #3905 "Add GHSA-j456 live probe; expand the GHSA-8mgp probe attack set" (commit a96715264, merged 2026-09-20, merge commit 84d987bf8); verdict on develop 2fa3f48fe: FIXED (WekaClassifier -l and -d refuse out-of-root model paths).

Release: none yet; no release tag contains 6a1760629.

### Summary

The `/sso/debug/callback` endpoint reflected identity-provider-controlled fields into an inline `<script>` block via `json.dumps`, which escapes JSON string syntax but not HTML context characters such as `</script>`. An IdP-returned string field containing `</script>` (for example a user-editable display name) closed the script block and executed attacker JavaScript in the proxy's origin.

### Impact

Reflected XSS on the LiteLLM proxy origin. The route required no authentication, so an attacker with an account on the configured IdP whose claims pass such strings through verbatim could complete the SSO flow themselves and deliver the resulting callback URL to a logged-in proxy admin. Scripts executing in the proxy origin can read the dashboard session cookie and act with the victim's privileges, up to full admin account takeover.

## Summary

An authenticated LiteLLM proxy user could read arbitrary local files from the proxy runtime by sending a crafted `vertex_ai_credentials` value to `/utils/transform_request`. The request-body safety blocklist rejected `vertex_credentials` but missed its alias `vertex_ai_credentials`, which let the value reach the Vertex AI credential loader and trigger a file read that is sent to an attacker-controlled URL.

## Impact

A low-privilege authenticated user (only `internal_user_viewer`, obtainable through SSO login on many deployments) could read any file readable by the LiteLLM process. Reading files such as `/proc/self/environ` can disclose `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` and provider API keys, so the impact can escalate to full proxy-admin control.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `1.95.0` or later. The fix adds the missing alias to the request-body blocklist, so no configuration change is needed once you upgrade. There is no reliable configuration workaround on affected versions.

### Summary

In Vikunja v2.6.0 the task position recalculation that runs when a saved filter view is created fails open when the requesting user has no accessible projects. Instead of aborting, the search that feeds the recalculation loses its project scope entirely and returns every task in the instance. The server then writes one `task_positions` row per task per view (four views per filter) into views owned by the requesting user, including rows that reference tasks of other tenants the user can never see. Any authenticated user can trigger this. The impact is a cross-tenant integrity violation, a single-request write amplification primitive that scales with instance size, and a violation of the invariant stated in the fix for GHSA-w39f-h553-h2mx that position writes are scoped by project read access.

### Details

Vikunja computes kanban and list ordering in a shared `task_positions` table keyed by `(task_id, project_view_id)`. When a saved filter is created, `SavedFilter.Create` (`pkg/models/saved_filters.go:130`) calls `CreateDefaultViewsForProject` (`pkg/models/project_view.go:816`) which, for every default view it creates, calls `RecalculateTaskPositions` with `addExistingTasksToView = true` (`pkg/models/project_view.go:447`).

`RecalculateTaskPositions` (`pkg/models/task_position.go:312`) builds a `TaskCollection` and, for filter views (`view.ProjectID < -1`), resets the project scope to zero and injects the saved filter's filter string. The scope of the subsequent search is derived from `getRelevantProjectsFromCollection` (`pkg/models/task_collection.go:188`), which for `ProjectID == 0` returns exactly the projects the requesting user can access.

Inside `dbTaskSearcher.Search` (`pkg/models/task_search.go`), the WHERE clause is assembled at line 632:

```go
cond := builder.And(builder.Or(projectIDCond, favoritesCond), where, filterCond)
```

`projectIDCond` is only set when `len(opts.projectIDs) > 0` and `favoritesCond` only when the caller opted into the favorites arm, which `RecalculateTaskPositions` never does. With zero accessible projects, an empty filter string (which produces no filter condition in `getTaskFiltersFromFilterString`) and no search string, all four children of the `builder.And` are invalid. go-xorm's condition builders silently drop invalid children, so the query becomes `SELECT ... FROM tasks` with no WHERE clause at all.

The result is written back unconditionally: the function deletes the view's position rows and bulk-inserts one row per returned task per view. Because the filter creation path runs this for four default views, one request writes `4 x total_task_count` rows, every one of them referencing tasks the requesting user has no relationship with, including tasks in other users' private projects.

Reaching the zero-project precondition does not require any bug beyond this one. `UpdateUserGeneralSettings` (`pkg/models/user_settings.go:105`) assigns `default_project_id` from the request body without validating that the referenced project exists or belongs to the caller. A user can therefore point their default project at any project id, which unblocks deleting their own Inbox (deletion is refused only while the Inbox is the default project, error 3012 in `pkg/models/error.go:482`). After the Inbox is gone, `getRawProjectsForUser` returns an empty list.

Two neighboring controls confirm the intended invariant exists elsewhere and is enforced in sibling paths. The event-driven filter update path gates candidate filters on the filter owner's access to each task's project (`matchTasksToViewsOfFilter`, introduced by commit `b1ad4063e7`), and the fix for GHSA-w39f-h553-h2mx validates position target views. The recalculation path on filter creation has no equivalent gate and contradicts the advisory statement that recalculation "aborts on its own project read-access check".

### PoC

> [vikunja-filter-empty-scope-cross-tenant-positions-PoC.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32740623/vikunja-filter-empty-scope-cross-tenant-positions-PoC.zip)

The attached archive contains `deployment/deploy.sh` (local Vikunja v2.6.0 on loopback with SQLite) and `poc/poc.sh`, which performs the full sequence:

1. Victim registers, creates a private project and a task.
2. Attacker registers, sets `default_project_id` to the victim's project via `PUT /api/v2/user/settings/general`, deletes their own Inbox, and now has zero accessible projects.
3. Control: `GET /api/v2/projects/{victim}` returns 403.
4. Attacker creates a saved filter with `{"filter":"","filter_include_nulls":true}`.
5. Verification: direct SQLite inspection shows `task_positions` rows referencing the victim's task in all four of the attacker's filter views.
6. Control: `GET /api/v2/projects/{filter_pseudo_project}/tasks` returns 0 items, so the written rows are not readable back through collection endpoints.

Result: 10 checks passed on two consecutive runs, each from a wiped database.

### Impact

An authenticated user, even one with no project access at all, causes the server to persist cross-tenant references: rows pointing at arbitrary other users' tasks are written into views the attacker controls. Task content is not exposed through the documented read paths (verified), so this is an integrity and availability issue rather than a direct disclosure:

- Cross-tenant integrity violation. The `task_positions` state of the attacker's views now encodes other tenants' objects, against the access model the rest of the code enforces.
- Write amplification and denial of service. One cheap request performs a full-table scan plus `4 x N` inserts, where N is the number of tasks in the instance. On an instance with 100,000 tasks that is 400,000 rows per request, and the request can be repeated without bound. CPU, IO and storage costs scale with instance size while attacker cost stays constant.

## Summary

`Remote.pull()` in GitPython forwards its positional `refspec` argument directly to the `git pull` child process while its unsafe-option guard inspects only keyword arguments. An application that passes attacker-influenced data as the `refspec` (for example a user-supplied branch or refspec parameter in a web or CI service) can supply an option-shaped value such as `--upload-pack=<command>`. The value bypasses the `unsafe_git_pull_options` check, is placed after the `--` separator on the `git pull` command line, and is executed as the upload-pack program for local-path or SSH transports. This yields arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the calling process using the documented default arguments (`allow_unsafe_options=False`).

## Root Cause

`Remote.pull()` is documented to reject dangerous options unless `allow_unsafe_options=True`, and `--upload-pack` is explicitly listed as such an option. The guard, however, only screens keyword arguments and never the positional `refspec`. The check builds its candidate list with `Git._option_candidates([], kwargs)`, passing an empty list in place of the positionals, so the `refspec` value is never compared against `unsafe_git_pull_options = ["--upload-pack"]`. The normalized `refspec` is then forwarded verbatim to the `git pull` invocation. The leading `--` separator that neutralizes an option-shaped refspec for `git fetch` and `git push` does not protect `git pull`, because `git pull` re-forwards its trailing positionals to an internal `git fetch` without re-inserting a `--` separator, so the positional becomes an option to that internal fetch.

```text
Affected function: git.remote.Remote.pull
Source: git/remote.py (guard at the check_unsafe_options call using _option_candidates([], kwargs); sink at the self.repo.git.pull("--", self, refspec, ...) invocation)
```

## Impact

An attacker who controls the `refspec` value passed to `Remote.pull()` achieves arbitrary operating-system command execution as the process invoking GitPython, with no additional privileges and no user interaction, on the default code path. Exploitation requires that the pulled remote uses a transport that runs upload-pack on the local side, namely a local filesystem path or SSH; over HTTPS the `--upload-pack` value is inert because the server ignores a client-supplied upload-pack program. This transport requirement narrows the population of vulnerable deployments but does not add work for the attacker once a vulnerable target is reached. Working checkouts commonly use local-path or SSH origins, so the exposed population is substantial.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Environment: GitPython from the affected source tree; system git 2.43.0.
The pulled origin uses a local filesystem transport (protocol.file.allow=always for git >= 2.38).
```

Reproduction steps:

1. Create an origin repository reachable over a local-path transport.
2. In a consumer repository, register that origin and call `Remote.pull()` with an attacker-controlled refspec.
3. Observe that the injected command executes.

```python
import git
repo = git.Repo("consumer")                 # has an origin using a local-path or ssh transport
origin = repo.remote("origin")
# Attacker-controlled refspec value; default arguments (allow_unsafe_options=False):
origin.pull(refspec="--upload-pack=touch /tmp/pwned; git-upload-pack")
```

```text
cmdline: git pull -v -- origin --upload-pack=touch /tmp/pwned; git-upload-pack
[attack]  marker created (RCE)      : True
[isolate] upload_pack passed as KWARG blocked : True   (only the positional refspec escapes)
[sibling] same value via git fetch  : safe            (pull-specific behavior)
[control] benign refspec            : safe
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An application calls `Remote.pull(refspec=<value>)` on the default path, where `<value>` is derived from attacker-influenced input such as a branch or refspec request parameter.
2. **Control:** The attacker supplies the string `--upload-pack=<command>; git-upload-pack`. The value passes through `Git._unpack_args`, which only flattens and stringifies it, preserving the option shape.
3. **Path:** The protocol loop calls `Git.check_unsafe_protocols` on the value, which only matches remote-helper transport URLs (a `<transport>::` form) and does not flag an `--upload-pack=` token.
4. **Guard:** The unsafe-option guard calls `check_unsafe_options(options=Git._option_candidates([], kwargs), ...)`. Because positionals are passed as an empty list, the positional `refspec` is never inspected against `unsafe_git_pull_options`.
5. **Primitive:** The value is forwarded to `git pull -v -- <remote> --upload-pack=<command>; git-upload-pack`; `git pull` re-forwards the positional to an internal `git fetch` without a `--` separator, so it is honored as the upload-pack program.
6. **Result:** For a local-path or SSH transport, git executes `<command>` as the upload-pack program, giving arbitrary command execution as the calling process user.

## Bypass Evidence

The relevant guard is `Remote.pull()`'s own `check_unsafe_options` call, present in the current released artifact. It is incomplete: it inspects `Git._option_candidates([], kwargs)`, which only considers keyword arguments, so the positional `refspec` is never checked. This was confirmed empirically: passing the identical value as the `upload_pack=` keyword argument raises `UnsafeOptionError`, while passing it as the positional `refspec` does not, proving that only the positional escapes the guard.

The `--` separator on the `git pull` command line was tested as a possible mitigation and refuted: with system git 2.43.0, `git pull -- <remote> '--upload-pack=<cmd>'` executed the injected command, while the identical value supplied to `git fetch -- ...` and `git push -- ...` did not execute, because those subcommands honor the `--` terminator whereas `git pull` re-forwards positionals to an internal fetch without one. The `check_unsafe_protocols` transport check was also examined and does not flag the `--upload-pack=` token because it has no `<transport>::` form. No prior published advisory for this package addresses `Remote.pull`, the fetch or pull refspec positional, or `--upload-pack` injection via a refspec; the closest accepted issue covers the same class (a positional argument escaping a keyword-only guard) in a different function and sink.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: pip (PyPI)`
- `Package: GitPython`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 3.1.30`
- `Latest release checked: 3.1.62 (PyPI); source verified against the 3.1.62 release tag`
- `Fix status: not fixed in any released version or on the development branch`

The keyword-only pull guard together with the positional `refspec` sink is present in every released tag from 3.1.30 through the latest release 3.1.62, verified by inspecting the shipped `git/remote.py` in each tagged artifact. Version 3.1.30 introduced the `unsafe_git_pull_options` guard; the affected range is stated from that boundary under the incomplete-guard framing. Releases before 3.1.30 forward the `refspec` positionally with no unsafe-option guard and no `--` separator and are also exploitable, but the range is stated conservatively from the guard-introduction boundary. No fixed release exists.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce the unsafe-option invariant on the positional `refspec`, not only on keyword arguments. The guard should build its candidate list from the actual forwarded positionals (for example by passing the normalized refspec list into `Git._option_candidates` alongside `kwargs`) so that an option-shaped `refspec` such as `--upload-pack=...` is rejected with `UnsafeOptionError` unless `allow_unsafe_options=True`. The same correction should be verified for any other reference or refspec forwarding path that relies on the keyword-only guard. As an interim mitigation without a code change, callers should validate or reject refspec values that begin with `-`, avoid passing untrusted data as the `refspec`, and prefer HTTPS remotes where a client-supplied upload-pack program is inert.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

### Summary
In affected versions, MCP servers reachable over HTTP put no limit on the size of a POST body or on the number of messages in a JSON-RPC batch. Large requests could exhaust the server's memory, and one long batch could block it from serving anyone else. No credentials were needed, unless your application authenticates requests before they reach the SDK.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if clients you do not fully trust can reach your server over Streamable HTTP. A body parser such as `express.json()` does not protect you, because it does not limit batch length. Servers that only use stdio are not affected.

Affected versions:

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.10.0 through 1.30.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.0.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/node` 2.0.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/hono` 2.0.0

### Fix
Upgrade to:

- 1.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.30.1 or later
- 2.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.1.0, `@modelcontextprotocol/node` 2.1.0 and `@modelcontextprotocol/hono` 2.0.1 or later. Upgrade every one you have installed.

Bodies over 4 MiB now get `413`, and batches over 100 messages get `400`. If your clients send larger bodies, raise the new `maxRequestBodySize` option.

If you cannot upgrade yet, cap request body size in a reverse proxy.

### Summary

Vikunja v2.6.0 introduced server-side sessions with revocation semantics: `DELETE /api/v2/user/sessions/{id}` documents "Revokes a specific session by its UUID", and enabling TOTP calls `DeleteAllUserSessions` to invalidate all sessions. The WebSocket endpoint accepts any cryptographically valid user JWT without ever resolving its `sid` (session id) claim against the sessions table. A connection authenticated before revocation stays authenticated and continues to receive live pushes indefinitely, and even brand-new WebSocket connections are accepted with a token whose session was deleted. The revocation feature therefore does not cover the WebSocket boundary at all.

### Details

User access JWTs carry a session reference: `NewUserJWTAuthtoken` (`pkg/modules/auth/auth.go:188`) sets `claims["sid"] = sessionID`, and the API login-session documentation describes the claim as tying the JWT to a server-side session. On the HTTP side nothing consumes the claim per request either (REST access tokens simply expire after their short TTL, a design the maintainers documented when fixing GHSA-96q5, and refresh tokens are correctly invalidated when the session row is deleted).

The WebSocket endpoint `GET /api/v2/ws` authenticates through the first client message. `Connection.handleAuth` (`pkg/websocket/connection.go:168`) validates the token exclusively with `auth.GetUserIDFromToken` (`pkg/modules/auth/auth.go:292`):

```go
func GetUserIDFromToken(tokenString string) (int64, error) {
	token, err := jwt.Parse(tokenString, func(_ *jwt.Token) (any, error) {
		return []byte(config.ServiceSecret.GetString()), nil
	})
	...
	typ, ok := claims["type"].(float64)
	if !ok || int(typ) != AuthTypeUser {
		return 0, jwt.ErrTokenInvalidClaims
	}
	...
}
```

The function verifies signature and token type only. No session lookup occurs anywhere in the WebSocket path, and no re-validation happens after the initial auth. Consequently:

1. A connection authenticated before `DELETE /api/v2/user/sessions/{id}` (or before TOTP enable, which runs `models.DeleteAllUserSessions`, `pkg/routes/api/v2/user_totp.go:208`) remains registered in the hub and keeps receiving every subscribed event, such as `notification.created` with the full notification object including comment, task and project content.
2. A new connection opened after the deletion, using the same pre-revocation token, authenticates successfully.
3. Session deletion is observable only in the REST surface. The user's session list empties, the refresh token dies on next use, but the WebSocket channel never notices.

For REST the exposure is bounded by the 10-minute access-token TTL. For WebSocket it is not: a connection lives until the client closes it, so a session the user believes revoked retains a live, server-pushed data channel with no time bound.

### PoC

> [vikunja-ws-auth-ignores-session-revocation-PoC.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32741065/vikunja-ws-auth-ignores-session-revocation-PoC.zip)

The attached archive contains `deployment/deploy.sh` (local Vikunja v2.6.0 on loopback with SQLite) and `poc/poc.sh` running `poc/poc.py`:

1. Victim registers and logs in. Second user registers for later interaction.
2. Control: the victim's WebSocket authenticates and subscribes to `notification.created`. Negative control: a garbage token is rejected with `invalid_token`.
3. Every victim session is deleted via `DELETE /api/v2/user/sessions/{id}` (the list afterwards reports 0 remaining).
4. Exploit A: a brand-new WebSocket connection authenticates successfully with the deleted-session token.
5. Exploit B: the second user comments on a task mentioning the victim. The victim's pre-revocation WebSocket connection receives the `notification.created` push with the full notification payload.

Result: 10 checks passed on two consecutive runs, each from a wiped database.

### Impact

Session revocation, the mechanism a user relies on when a device is lost or a token is suspected stolen, silently excludes the WebSocket channel. A stolen or leaked access token can be converted into a push channel that survives every revocation action available to the user, including TOTP enrollment whose documented purpose is invalidating all sessions, and keeps delivering the victim's notifications (comment mentions, task and project metadata) until the attacker chooses to disconnect. The fix is to resolve the `sid` claim against the sessions table during `handleAuth` and to re-validate or drop hub connections when their session is deleted.
items.title: Vikunja: WebSocket authentication ignores server-side session state, so revoked sessions keep receiving live pushes

## Summary

Nodemailer's SMTP client applies four regular expressions to a peer's EHLO response to detect the supported SASL mechanisms. Each pattern uses an alternation with two overlapping whitespace-matching sub-patterns, which produces quadratic (O(n^2)) backtracking whenever the mechanism name is absent from the line. A malicious or MITM SMTP server that answers EHLO with `250-AUTH` followed by a long whitespace-only run and a non-matching token blocks the Node.js event loop for tens of seconds to hours during a pre-authentication handshake. No authentication to the target SMTP server is required, and any application that connects to an attacker-influenced host is affected.

## Root Cause

Each of the four AUTH mechanism regexes in `SMTPConnection._actionEHLO` contains the sub-pattern `(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)` before the mechanism literal. `[^\n]*` and the trailing `\s+` both match whitespace and can consume the same characters, so when the mechanism literal is absent, the regex engine must try every partition of the whitespace run between `[^\n]*` and `\s+` before failing. The four regexes run unconditionally on every EHLO response, with no length cap, no shape validation, and no early rejection before the engine enters the ambiguous alternation.

```text
Component: nodemailer (npm), SMTP client
Function:  SMTPConnection._actionEHLO
Location:  src/smtp-connection/index.ts, lines 2162, 2167, 2172, 2177
Patterns:  /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)PLAIN/i
           /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)LOGIN/i
           /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)CRAM-MD5/i
           /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)XOAUTH2/i
```

## Impact

Algorithmic-complexity denial of service against any Node.js process that opens an SMTP connection to an attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced host. Node.js is single threaded, so the process stalls entirely while the regex engine backtracks: no other requests are served, no timers fire, and the built-in socket timeout (10 minutes) cannot interrupt synchronous JavaScript. A 4,000-character whitespace run inside a single continuation line already blocks each regex for tens of seconds; the client bounds a response at 1 MB, which leaves headroom for blocking runs measured in hours across the four patterns. Two realistic attacker positions reach the sink pre-authentication: a hosted mailer that lets tenants configure their own SMTP server, and any network-adjacent attacker able to man-in-the-middle a cleartext SMTP connection (including before STARTTLS negotiation).

## Proof of Concept

The PoC exercises the exact four regexes copied from `src/smtp-connection/index.ts` against a synthesized `250-AUTH<whitespace>NOMATCH` line, so no live SMTP server is needed to reproduce the timing.

```text
Runtime:      Node.js >= 20
Dependencies: none
Invocation:   node poc.js
```

```javascript
'use strict';

const AUTH_REGEXES = [
    /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)PLAIN/i,
    /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)LOGIN/i,
    /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)CRAM-MD5/i,
    /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)XOAUTH2/i,
];

function bench(n) {
    const line = '250-AUTH' + ' '.repeat(n) + 'NOMATCH';
    const start = Date.now();
    for (const re of AUTH_REGEXES) re.test(line);
    return Date.now() - start;
}

for (const n of [500, 1000, 2000, 3000]) {
    console.log(`n=${n}  four-regex time=${bench(n)} ms`);
}

const control = '250-AUTH PLAIN LOGIN CRAM-MD5 XOAUTH2';
const t0 = Date.now();
for (const re of AUTH_REGEXES) re.test(control);
console.log(`well-formed control  four-regex time=${Date.now() - t0} ms`);
```

```text
n=500   four-regex time=914 ms
n=1000  four-regex time=1348 ms
n=2000  four-regex time=10558 ms
n=3000  four-regex time=35251 ms
well-formed control  four-regex time=0 ms
```

Doubling the whitespace run multiplies the wall time by roughly four, which matches the expected O(n^2) growth. The well-formed control shows that a normal EHLO response is parsed in effectively zero time.

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** The victim application, or any dependent that uses `nodemailer` to send mail, opens a TCP or TLS connection to an SMTP host the attacker controls. This happens automatically for multi-tenant mailers whose tenants configure their own outbound SMTP server, and for any client whose plaintext SMTP session can be intercepted by a network-adjacent attacker before STARTTLS negotiation.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the bytes returned in response to `EHLO`. In particular, the attacker chooses the length and content of every `250-` continuation line up to the client's 1 MB response cap.
3. **Path:** Socket bytes are reassembled by `_onData`, decoded by `_processResponse`, and dispatched to `_actionEHLO`. On the first EHLO after the greeting (malicious server with no STARTTLS), on the second EHLO after a successful STARTTLS upgrade, or on the first EHLO when `ignoreTLS` is set, control reaches the AUTH detection block near the end of `_actionEHLO`.
4. **Guard:** The only bounds on this path are `maxResponseSize` (1 MB by default) and the 421 or non-2xx status-code check. Neither prevents O(n^2) backtracking: 4,000 whitespace characters already block each regex for tens of seconds, well below the 1 MB cap. No length, shape, or sanitization check runs before the regexes.
5. **Primitive:** Four `RegExp.prototype.test` calls execute against the crafted line, each entering catastrophic backtracking because `[^\n]*` and `\s+` share the whitespace alphabet and the mechanism literal never matches.
6. **Result:** The Node.js event loop is blocked for the duration of the four regex evaluations. All other work in the process, including timers, unrelated requests, keep-alive traffic, and the SMTP socket timeout itself, is suspended until the regexes return.

## Bypass Evidence

The only response-side protection in this code path is `maxResponseSize`, introduced by the fix for GHSA-4g23-2xm8-66gc (commit `f2d82fa`). That fix targeted quadratic reassembly of long multiline replies inside `_onData` and left the AUTH regex evaluation in `_actionEHLO` untouched. `maxResponseSize` does not prevent this issue: at 4,000 whitespace characters, roughly 0.4 percent of the default 1 MB cap, a single continuation line already blocks each of the four regexes for tens of seconds. No status-code or length gate rejects the payload before the regex engine enters the ambiguous alternation, and Node.js's single-threaded event loop cannot service the socket timeout while a synchronous `test()` call is running. Two other recent linear-time fixes in this project (the addressparser fallback for GHSA-v53p-9fqp-m79j and the DKIM header unfolding for GHSA-39m8-27wv-hr27) address entirely different modules and inputs and do not touch the AUTH mechanism regexes.

## Affected Versions

- **Ecosystem:** `npm`
- **Package:** `nodemailer`
- **Confirmed affected range:** `>= 3.0.0, <= 10.0.12`
- **Latest release checked:** `10.0.12` ([npm registry](https://registry.npmjs.org/nodemailer/10.0.12))
- **Fix status:** 10.0.13

The four AUTH mechanism regexes were introduced when the SMTP client was bundled into `nodemailer` at 3.0.0 (previously a separate `smtp-connection` package). The vulnerable alternation `(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)` is present, unchanged, in every published release from 3.0.0 (`lib/smtp-connection/index.js`) through 10.0.12 (`dist/esm/smtp-connection/index.js` and `dist/cjs/smtp-connection/index.js`). A later refactor added a leading `[ -]` character class but did not alter the ambiguous inner alternation. No release, and no development branch inspected at the current HEAD (`30e4cfd`), contains a fix for this pattern.

## Suggested Fix

Replace the four backtracking regexes with a non-ambiguous parse of the AUTH extension. The invariant the fix must enforce is that mechanism detection runs in time linear in the response length regardless of whitespace shape. A minimal approach: match the AUTH extension value with a single non-backtracking pattern (for example, `/[ -]AUTH(?:\s+|=)([^\r\n]*)/i`) and then check for each mechanism name against the whitespace-split tokens with a `Set` lookup or `includes`. The fix must cover both continuation forms (`250-AUTH ...` and `250 AUTH ...`) and both delimiters (space and `=`), and must handle the "AUTH advertised with no mechanisms" case without walking the whitespace run. As an interim mitigation, callers who never connect to an untrusted SMTP peer can restrict SMTP endpoints to a known allowlist; this does not help clients that must interoperate with arbitrary user-configured servers or with any cleartext SMTP path exposed to a network-adjacent attacker before STARTTLS.

---

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use `@better-auth/drizzle-adapter` from 1.6.17 through versions before 1.7.7 (including the 1.7.0 prereleases from beta.6 through rc.6) or `@better-auth/kysely-adapter` 1.6.17 through 1.6.31, and keep rate-limit records in a PostgreSQL database.

All of these must be true:

- Rate limiting is enabled.
- Rate-limit records are stored in the database.
- The database is PostgreSQL, used through one of the adapter versions above.

You are not affected if you store rate-limit records in memory (the default) or in secondary storage.

## Summary

Database-backed rate limiting on PostgreSQL can let a burst of concurrent requests go over the configured maximum. When many requests arrive at the same time, several of them can pass the limit check together. This weakens the rate limit on password sign-in, two-factor verification, one-time codes, password resets, and other rate-limited endpoints.

## Impact

An attacker who sends many requests at once can make more attempts than the application allows.

The issue does not bypass password or one-time-code validation. It does not directly compromise an account. The number of extra attempts is limited by the number of concurrent database connections, the number of application instances, and the rate-limit window.

## Patches

`@better-auth/kysely-adapter` is fixed in 1.7.0. Upgrade to 1.7.0 or later.

The Drizzle fix is merged for the planned `@better-auth/drizzle-adapter` 1.7.7 release. That package is not available yet. Upgrade `better-auth` and the installed Drizzle adapter together when 1.7.7 is available. No database schema or public API migration is required.

## Workarounds

- Store rate-limit records in secondary storage.
- Use a custom rate-limit storage that checks and increments the counter in one atomic step. An atomic step cannot be interrupted by another request.
- Enforce the intended limit at an upstream layer, such as a reverse proxy or gateway.

In-memory storage also avoids this issue. However, each application instance keeps its own counter, so it may not enforce one shared limit in multi-instance or serverless deployments.

Rustls accepted TLS 1.3 handshake messages sent at the wrong encryption level when they followed a key-changing message in the same record. The handshake transcript is still authenticated, so a network-position attacker cannot use this to alter or complete a handshake; the practical effect is that a peer could send handshake messages that should be encrypted in plaintext without rustls rejecting the connection.

This issue affects rustls versions 0.23.13 through 0.23.44 inclusive.

# Original report
### Summary
Rustls (tested version 0.23.44, and it appears still an issue on latest master though I have not tested this) accepts a TLS 1.3 server flight where a plaintext EncryptedExtensions is packed into the same record as the ServerHello.

This is very similar to Go's CVE-2025-61730 fixed in https://github.com/golang/go/commit/5046bdf8a612b35a2c1a9e168054c1d5c65e7dd7

### Details
It appears `Deframer::aligned` considers itself aligned as long as all messages remaining in the buffer are complete. Rustls processes the ServerHello, installs the handshake keys, then pulls the complete (plaintext) EncryptedExtensions out of the buffer.

This is insufficient per RFC 8446 section 5.1's

> Handshake messages MUST NOT span key changes.  Implementations MUST verify that all messages immediately preceding a key change align with a record boundary; if not, then they MUST terminate the connection with an "unexpected_message" alert.  Because the ClientHello, EndOfEarlyData, ServerHello, Finished, and KeyUpdate messages can immediately precede a key change, implementations MUST send these messages in alignment with a record boundary.

### Impact
An on path attacker can inject plaintext messages that are accepted.

### Tool Use Disclosure
This was discovered by a new TLS/DTLS test suite currently under construction. The specific testcase was inspired by the Go CVE. Other tested implementations (Botan, OpenSSL, BoringSSL, Go, wolfSSL) reject this protocol flow. Daybreak Blue reviewed the rustls code to identify probable root cause.
items.title: Rustls: TLS 1.3 handshake messages incorrectly accepted across encryption level boundaries
